items.name: Zolo Azania
items.was: Zolo Agona Azania is a New Afrikan activist and artist convicted of the 1981 killing of a Gary, Indiana police lieutenant during a bank robbery. He spent years on death row before his death sentences were twice overturned for misconduct; he was resentenced and ultimately paroled around 2017 after more than three decades inside.
items.now:
Zolo Azania is a former Black Panther convicted of a 1981 bank robbery that left a Gary, Indiana cop dead. He was arrested miles away from the incident as he was walking, unarmed, down the street. After a trial plagued with injustices, Zolo was given the death penalty. After years of campaigning and several orders to stop his execution, the death penalty sentence was finally dropped. Zolo still adamantly maintains innocence.

At the time of his arrest, Zolo was a well-known activist in his hometown of Gary, Indiana. He was an ex-con who had grown up in extreme poverty, but he was also the valedictorian of his CETA federal job training class and had received a scholarship to Purdue University just prior to his arrest. An artist and writer, he was involved in the campaign to make Martin Luther King’s birthday a national holiday and had designed a button used by campaigners in Gary.

During Zolo’s trial, the prosecution intimidated witnesses, suppressed favorable evidence, presented false eyewitness and expert testimony, and denied him the right to speak or present motions on his own behalf.

The two other men charged and convicted with Zolo received sentences of 60 years. But Zolo’s political history and beliefs were used to paint an unfair and inaccurate picture of him and he received the death penalty for a crime he was not involved in.

Since the trial, the battle to save Zolo’s life has successfully resisted several attempts to follow through with the death penalty conviction. On October 17, 2008 after two overturned judge rulings barring his execution, the State of Indiana finally abandoned their 27-year campaign to execute Zolo Azania. Zolo no longer faces the death penalty! This is a real victory for all Zolo’s supporters and all of those who oppose the death penalty.

As part of the agreement, Judge Altice imposed two sentences instead of the death penalty. He sentenced Zolo to 60 years for the shooting death of a policeman. Zolo should serve 30 years of that sentence and the 27 years he has already served will be deducted from that, leaving 3 more years to serve on that sentence. The shooting happened during a bank robbery and for that robbery, which Zolo also has denied being involved in, he was sentenced to 14 years. Zolo should serve 7 years of that sentence. The 7 years may be reduced by 3 years if Zolo obtains a college degree while in prison. Zolo has been denied the ability to earn a college degree in the past because he had been sentenced to be executed. Before his arrest on these charges in 1981, Zolo had received a scholarship to Purdue University.

Life in Prison

Since his arrest Zolo has fought the charges against him from his prison cell, often on death row. His tireless efforts have exposed the unfair and racist way his case has been handled by the authorities. He has defended his own rights and the rights of other prisoners winning the respect of fellow prisoners and jailers alike. His victories, overturning his death sentence twice, have set precedents cited by other prisoners.

Zolo was released from prison on Monday, February 6, 2017!

items.name: Abdelhaleem Ashqar
items.was: Abdelhaleem Ashqar, a Palestinian-born former Howard University business professor, was acquitted of racketeering but convicted of criminal contempt and obstruction for refusing to testify before a grand jury investigating Hamas, saying he would not "live as a traitor or a collaborator." Sentenced in 2007 to more than eleven years (sharply enhanced as terrorism), he was released around 2017 and faced deportation.
items.now: Dr. Abdelhaleem Ashqar was a Howard University Professor and Palestinian activist who fled to the United States in 1981 as a college student after being arrested and beaten by authorities for participating in a political demonstration at Birzeit University against Israel’s military occupation. In the United States he finished his education and founded the al-Aqsa Educational Fund which was a charity that funded schooling initiatives in Palestine. Dr. Ashqar would give frequent lectures and speeches about the plight of the Palestinian people. Due to transferring large sums of money to the Middle East the account of his foundation was flagged as a potential money laundering account but was cleared by the FBI, though after consulting Israeli intelligence the FBI was told the money could be being used for terrorism. The FBI bugged Dr. Ashqars phone but found no evidence he was involved in terrorism. The FBI set up a meeting with Ashqar where they asked him to become an undercover informant and make statements to them that other Palestinian activists were Hamas members. He refused and in 1998 was subpoenaed Ashqar, to testify in a grand jury as part of the FBI’s investigation into a network of alleged Hamas financiers in the United States, Ashqar refused to testify and spent 6 months held in solitary confinement. In September 2003, he was jailed for civil contempt for two months after refusing again to testify in an investigation One year later, a grand jury returned indictments against Ashqar for obstructing justice, along with indictments against Marzook and Muhammad Salah, a Chicago-based Palestinian activist who had earlier been arrested by Israel and was allegedly tortured into confessing membership to Hamas. Prosecutors also charged Ashqar with being part of a conspiracy to advance Hamas’s criminal actions by financing the militant group. Ashqar was found not guilty on charges of financing Hamas. was convicted for obstructing justice over his refusal to give testimony in November 2007 instead sentenced him to 11 years in prison. After being released he spent the next 18 months in immigration detention finally released in December 2018 But after about six months at home, Ashqar was back in prison. His lawyer feared that ICE still wanted to deport him to Israel. Jurors acquitted Ashqar of racketeering conspiracy, but was still sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in prison for refusing to testify before a grand jury that was investigating money- laundering and non-profits funding “terrorist” organizations. These charges are broad sweeping and are the same types of charges being brought against Dr. Dhafir. http://www.free-ashqar.org/

items.name: Maliki Shakur Latine
items.was: Maliki Shakur Latine, born in the Bronx in 1953, was a member of the Black Panther Party and the Black Liberation Army. Sentenced in 1981 to 25 years to life for the attempted murder of a New York City police officer, he was freed in 2016 after 37 years.
items.now:
Maliki Shakur Latine is a person who has consistently acted, studied, and worked for the betterment of his community. He is a very peaceful and deeply spiritual person who spends his time helping others. In his youth, Mr. Latine made a series of mistakes that put him behind bars for much of his life. He has educated himself and served his community while serving his time in New York State correctional facilities.

Early Life

Maliki Shakur Latine was born in the Bronx on August 23, 1953. An early sense of spirituality and community responsibility as a young Muslim lead him to join the Nation of Islam and then the Bronx Chapter of the Black Panther Party. He was taking political education classes, serving in community programs, and developing a life-long interest in history, philosophy, and spirituality. Due to COINTELPRO targeting the BPP, many went underground in the 70's as did Maliki.

Legal Case

Unfortunately, on July 3rd, 1979, a traffic accident lead to a tragic event involving Maliki Shakur Latine, police officers, and others. The altercation resulted in arrests and some arrestees became career informants for the government. A month later, on August 7, 1979, Maliki Latine was arrested in St. Albans, Queens. On October 1, 1981, Maliki Shakur Latine was sentenced to twenty-five to life for attempted murder in the first degree and seven and one half to fifteen years for assault in the first degree.

Life in Prison

In prison Mr. Latine continued his community work and study, through increasingly wise, mature and peaceful means. He has continued to study philosophy, ancient civilizations, Islam, and many other topics. Mr. Latine has completed Aggression Replacement Training (ART), Abuse Treatment (ASAT). He has served as a program assistant and an electrician’s helper. He’s taken vocational classes and received his GED in 2011. He has not received any disciplinary action in the past six years. He has served on Inmate Liaison Committees at several facilities and has taught classes on reentry and release. He writes letters and receives visits so as to connect with his community, give advice, and make contributions. Unfortunately, Mr. Latine has also suffered from his life-long multiple food allergies and has been unable to receive an optimally appropriate diet while in prison, despite multiple recommendations from allergists, physicians and other health professionals.

He was released on parole on December 6, 2016 on his seventh appearance.

items.name: Sekou Kambui
items.was: Sekou Cinque Kambui (William Turk) was a civil-rights and Black Panther organizer in Alabama. Accused of two 1975 killings in cases marked by allegations of coerced witnesses, he served about 40 years and was paroled on June 18, 2014.
items.now: Sekou Kambui was a Civil Rights activist with the Southern Christian Leadership Council (SCLC), Congress for Racial Equality (CORE) and the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC). When Sekou was 19 years old, he became affiliated with the Black Panther Party and Republic of New Afrika. In the 1970s, Sekou spent most of his time community organizing in Birmingham, Alabama with the Alabama Black Liberation Front, the Inmates for Action, and the Afro-Amerikan People’s Party. Because of his activism in the Civil Rights movement, he was watched closely by the FBI’s counterintelligence program entitled COINTELPRO, and was subsequently profiled and pulled over on January 2, 1975 for allegedly running a yield sign and/or speeding. During the traffic stop the officer found a pistol in Sekou’s vehicle, and after strong suspicion by the officer that it was the weapon listed as stolen during a Tuscaloosa, Alabama murder, Sekou was taken into custody and charged for the murders of the two white men; a KKK official and a billionaire oilman. During his trial defense witnesses provided alibi testimony for Kambui during the time of the murder leading to a hung jury only for those witnesses to later flee the state after being threatened by Birmingham Police. Leaving Kambui with no defense during his second trial. Throughout both trials, major witnesses admitted that they had been coerced into testifying falsely against Sekou and were repeatedly visited by certain members of the Tuscaloosa County and Jefferson County Sheriff’s Department and were deliberately coached on what to say during their testimonies. Sekou was never placed at or near the crime scene, the real murder weapon was never found, nor was there ever any direct evidence to connect him to the murders.

items.name: Delbert Africa
items.was:
A leader of the Philadelphia MOVE organization, which The Black Panther Vol. 18 no.8 (1978) reports was under police siege by the Rizzo administration, with members accused of weapons offenses and two convicted federally of making explosive devices. He was later beaten by police at MOVE's 1978 eviction and imprisoned for decades. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v18 no.8; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]

Delbert Orr Africa is a member of MOVE, the Philadelphia-based Black liberation and back-to-nature group founded by John Africa, and one of the "MOVE 9." Following the August 8, 1978 armed police confrontation at MOVE's Powelton Village house — in which Officer James Ramp was killed — the nine surviving adult members were convicted of third-degree murder in 1980 and each sentenced to 30 to 100 years. After about four decades inside, consistently maintaining innocence, the MOVE 9 members were granted parole between 2018 and 2020.
items.now:
Delbert Samuel Orr Africa was a Black Panther and MOVE member.
Orr joined the Chicago Black Panther Party (C-BPP) in the early months of 1969, enrolled in their mandatory six-week Marxist and Socialist political education program, and briefly became its Minister of Information. 

After the December 4, 1969 police/FBI assassination of C-BPP chairman Fred Hampton and Mark Clark, Orr fled to Philadelphia. He met John Africa, formally Vincent Lopez Leaphart, and his Community Action Movement (MOVE) in March 1970, and within months he joined, making Africa his last name. MOVE was a Black liberation, naturalist group that embraced environmentalism, sustainability, and anti-capitalism.

In May 1973, MOVE purchased a communal Powelton Village home, near Drexel University. John appointed Delbert as Minister of Confrontation and Security after the formerly peaceful organization was driven to armed self-defense in 1977 to counter years of judicial subjugation, state violence, incarcerations, and fines. Tensions escalated in March 1976 when Philadelphia police stomped to death a MOVE infant, Life Africa.

On August 8, 1978 the police evicted MOVE from their house. In the confrontation friendly fire killed Officer James J. Ramp, and an unarmed and shirtless Delbert Africa was savagely beaten.  Media outlets nationally beamed the video-recorded brutal assault, which resulted in a cracked cheekbone, broken right-jaw, fractured eye-socket, and multiple lacerations/contusions. In 1981, despite an unidentified shooter, inconsistencies, and absence of intent, Delbert Africa and eight MOVE members were sentenced to 30-100 years in prison for Ramp’s death.

On May 13, 1985, police bombed MOVE’s Cobbs Creek row home that resulted in the murder of eleven of its members and 250 Philadelphians becoming unhoused. The deceased included Delesha (Delitia) Melissa Orr Africa, the twelve-year-old daughter of Delbert and Janet Holloway Africa. As in the 1978 police beating, no officers were criminally prosecuted.

Delbert Africa spent forty-one years in prison before being released in January 2020. For six years of his incarceration, Delbert Africa was put in an infamous solitary confinement wing known by prisoners as the “dungeon”. His isolation was imposed because he refused to have his dreadlocks cut – part of the MOVE philosophy. He died of prostate and bone cancer six months later on June 15, 2020 at the age of 74. In April 2021, Princeton and University of Pennsylvania apologized for their unethical use and possession of Delesha and Tree Africa’s remains.

items.name: William "Lefty" Gilday
items.was: William "Lefty" Gilday was a minor league baseball player and anti-war activist who served as a member of Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) and the Weather Underground. On September 23, 1970, Gilday and other members were involved in a bank expropriation attempting to fund the anti-war movement which ended with a police officer being killed. Gilday was tried and found guilty for the killing of the Boston police officer. He was sentenced to death but his sentence was later reduced to life imprisonment. Gilday died in prison in 2011.
items.now:
William “Lefty” Gilday was an anti-war activist who died as an incarcerated elder for his role in revolutionary actions against the Vietnam War. He was a former minor league baseball player from Amesbury, Massachusetts, who, while in his early to mid-thirties, was arrested and imprisoned on robbery charges. While imprisoned he met up with Stanley Bond, a Vietnam helicopter pilot also imprisoned on robbery charges. The two became friends and after their release, both entered into the Student Tutor Education Program (STEP), a program designed to help former inmates enter into university level education. Gilday enrolled into Boston’s Northeastern University with another fellow inmate, Robert Valeri; soon Gilday, Bond and Valeri became involved in the student movements of the 1960’s, joining organizations such as Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) and the Weather Underground. 

On September 23, 1970, Gilday and other college students (Bond, Valeri, Susan Saxe, and Katherine Powers) were involved in a bank expropriation attempting to the fund the anti-war movement which ended with a police officer killed. Gilday was tried and found guilty for the killing of the Boston police officer. He was sentenced to death but his sentence was later reduced to life imprisonment. Among the others involved in the action, Valeri became an accomplice to the state for a reduced sentence, Saxe and Powers both became fugitives before serving their time and getting released, and Bond died as part of an explosion in the jail.

Lefty, the last one remaining in prison, passed away on September 10, 2011 from dementia and Parkinson's at age 82. At the end of his life, he was placed in an isolation cell — a “medical bubble” —  for throwing an empty milk carton at a guard. He spent the last months of his life alone, separated by a window from medical staff, who placed manila folders across the glass so they didn’t have to look at him.

items.name: Tsutomu Shirosaki
items.was: Tsutomu Shirosaki was a member of the Japanese Red Army convicted in U.S. federal court in 1998 over the 1986 rocket attack on the U.S. embassy in Jakarta, and sentenced to 30 years. Released for good behavior in January 2015, he was deported to Japan, where he was tried and imprisoned again. He died at Fuchu Prison in Tokyo on July 20, 2024, at age 76.
items.now: Tsutomu Shirosaki was a Japanese university student who in the 1970s participated in a string of robberies that aimed to secure funds for Japanese radical groups. Tsutomu was arrested in 1971, and sentenced to ten years in prison for his participation. In 1977 the Japanese Red Army hijacked Japan Airlines Flight 472 and demanded the Japanese government release political prisoners held in Japan in exchange for the passengers. Tsutomu was one of the prisoners who was released and flown to Algeria by the Japanese government to swap him for the hostages. Without a passport or the ability to travel, Tsutomu ended up being settled in Lebanon. On May 14, 1986, two mortar-styled rockets were fired into the U.S. Embassy compound in Jakarta, Indonesia, there were no injuries. A group calling itself the Anti-Imperialist International Brigade (AIIB) claimed responsibility for the attack. Seven weeks later, the Japanese government claimed that they had found a fingerprint of Tsutomu Shirosaki in the hotel room where the rockets were launched from. During the time of the attack, Tsutomu was still in Lebanon and could not leave the country. After the 1993 Oslo Accords, Tsutomu was forced to flee Lebanon due to changing political climate. On September 21, 1996, local police in Nepal arrested Tsutomu after the National Security Agency tapped the phones of his friends to find his location. He was handed over to the FBI and extradited to the United States to stand trial for the Embassy attack. Tsutomu asserted his fingerprint had been planted at the scene from his arrest file which Japanese police had been known to do in order to frame suspects since the 1970s. He was convicted of the attack and sentenced to 30 years in prison.

items.name: James Johnson
items.was: James Johnson is an Oregon prisoner who, after being jailed as a non-political ("social") prisoner, became an active anti-authoritarian organizer within Oregon's prisons and faced sustained retaliation from prison authorities (per the Anarchist Black Cross, 2003). He is a different person from the New York prisoner Mohaman Koti, formerly known as James Carter Johnson.
items.now:
Mohamman Koti, formerly known as James Carter Johnson, was a Black ____ and an innocent man who, at the time of his incarceration, was the oldest man in the NY prison system (age 87). In 1978, Koti after a shootout with the police in Manhattan that led to an officer's injury. Koti turned down a plea offer, which would have given him a prison sentence of 7.5 to 15 years in state prison. Instead, he proceeded to trial and received a sentence of 25 years to life. Koti would go on to suffer from Myasthenia Gravis, a disease that causes his immune system to attack itself, as well as asthma, prostate cancer, diabetes, and heart disease. Koti was regularly hospitalized.

Ten years after Koti was eligible for parole, he was profiled in a 2013 New York Times column about prisoners over the age of 60 who are denied release based on their original crime, instead of an accurate assessment of the threat they pose. Koti suffered from several medical problems and used a wheelchair, but he was still found to be at risk of committing another crime. He was ultimately granted parole in September 2014, but because of a pending bank robbery charge from the time of his arrest, he was ordered to serve an additional year in prison at a federal medical center in Butner, North Carolina. Mr. Koti was released from New York State custody in 2015 and picked up by the Federal BOP and remanded to Butner Medical Facility in North Carolina to complete a prior sentence.

He was released in 2016 and passed away just two months later in a nursing home in Staten Island.

items.name: John Graham
items.was: John Graham (John Boy Patton), a Southern Tutchone member of the American Indian Movement from the Yukon, was extradited from Canada and convicted in 2010 of the 1975 murder of AIM activist Anna Mae Aquash, drawing a mandatory life sentence. He maintains his innocence; the case remains bitterly contested within the movement. He is held at the South Dakota State Penitentiary.
items.now:
John Graham is a member of the American Indian Movement and a Native American activist. Graham has spoken in multiple countries on Native rights to raise awareness of the impact of uranium mining in Canada on Indigenous Canadians. 

On December 10th, 2010 a South Dakota jury found John Graham guilty of felony murder in the death of American Indian Movement (AIM) member Anna Mae Aquash. Aquash was murdered in the 1970s in an execution-style killing in South Dakota. There are still many unanswered questions related to Aquash's death. Candy Hamilton testified that Aquash told her that FBI Agent David Price had threatened that "he would see that she died" if she didn't cooperate with his investigation of the Pine Ridge shootings of two FBI agents, indicating that the state might have had a role in her murder. Meanwhile, Aquash's daughters Denise and Debbie believe that high-ranking AIM leaders ordered the death of their mother due to fears of her being an informant.

Graham has said that she was his friend and comrade and continues to maintain his innocence. The John Graham Defense Committee attests that Graham did not receive a fair trial by virtue of the fact that the jury was prevented from access to the background of the case, and from hearing any of Mr. Graham’s witnesses, such that his conviction was based solely on the uncorroborated testimony of co-conspirators and informants.

items.name: Patrice Lumumba Ford
items.was: Patrice Lumumba Ford, a former Portland city intern, was one of the "Portland Seven" — a group that attempted to travel to Afghanistan after the September 11 attacks to aid the Taliban. He refused to cooperate with the government and pleaded guilty in 2003 to seditious conspiracy, drawing an 18-year sentence. He was released in 2018.
items.now:
Patrice Lumumba Ford is a Muslim activist and son of a former Black Panther leader who was planning a trip to volunteer in Afghani refugee camps.  He was arrested in 2002 and falsely accused of attempting to travel to Afghanistan to aid the Taliban. He refused to cooperate with the government and was sentenced to eighteen years in prison (avoiding a possible life sentence) after pleading guilty to seditious conspiracy and levying war against American and allied forces.
Accused of membership in a terrorist group dubbed the Portland Seven, members of which attempted to travel to Afghanistan shortly after 9/11 in order to aid the Taliban. He refused to cooperate with the government and was sentenced to eighteen years in prison (avoiding a possible life sentence) after pleading guilty to seditious conspiracy and levying war against American and allied forces. Patrice Lumumba Ford is Ford’s birth name — he is named after Patrice Lumumba. Ford’ s father, Kent Ford, had been a local leader in the Black Panther Party in the 1960s. A family friend and political activist, Kathleen Sadat commented that “Lumumba was raised by people who taught that we exist in a multicultural world and the trick is learning how to get along with other people, not to destroy them.”

items.name: H. C. White
items.was: H. C. White, an YWW member, served a prison sentence in San Quentin.
items.now: James “Angry Bird” White is a Native American activist and member of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe who became known for his participation in resistance to the Dakota Access Pipeline protests in North Dakota. White was involved in protecting water and sacred sites as part of the #NoDAPL movement opposing the construction of the pipeline on Indigenous land. Federal prosecutors charged him and several other water protectors with offenses including civil disorder and related federal charges arising from protests in 2016. He entered a plea agreement in 2018, under which he received time served plus probation/home confinement rather than an extended prison sentence; other protesters in the broader case received varying terms of incarceration. White worked in security at the protest camps and has been described by supporters as part of Indigenous resistance to environmental harm.

items.name: Mufid Abdulqader
items.was: Mufid Abdulqader was a volunteer performer and fundraiser for the Holy Land Foundation, convicted in 2008 in the foundation's material-support case and sentenced to 20 years. He was released on December 12, 2024 after 16 years.
items.now: Mufid  Abdulqader was a Palestinian born United States citizen who worked as a senior project manager in the public works and transportation Department for the City of Dallas Texas and spent his free time volunteering for the Holy Land Foundation. The largest Islamic charity in the United States. The Israeli government lobbied for years to have it shut down, and after 9/11, President Bush signed an executive order declaring the group a domestic terrorist organization. The government arrested its employees and argued that by building infrastructure in Palestine with charity money, it negated the need for the elected government of Palestine, which was Hamas, to build their own infrastructure. Thus, they could use the money they would have spent on hospitals instead on terrorism. After a number of mistrials and acquittals, the US government was able to convict 5 members of the board, including Abdulqader, who was sentenced to 20 years in jail.

items.name: Carl Braden
items.was:
Carl Braden was a Louisville, Kentucky journalist and civil-rights organizer with the Southern Conference Educational Fund. In 1954 he and his wife Anne Braden bought a house in an all-white Louisville suburb and transferred it to a Black family, Andrew and Charlotte Wade; after the house was bombed, it was Braden — not the bombers — who was prosecuted, convicted of sedition, and briefly imprisoned before the conviction was voided. In 1958 he was subpoenaed by the House Un-American Activities Committee in Atlanta and refused, on First Amendment grounds, to answer questions about his associations. Convicted of contempt of Congress, he appealed; the Supreme Court affirmed the conviction 5–4 in Braden v. United States (decided together with Wilkinson v. United States) in 1961, and he served time in federal prison.

Braden was first prosecuted in 1954, when Kentucky charged him with sedition after he and his wife Anne helped an African American family, the Wades, purchase a house in a segregated Louisville neighborhood. He received fifteen years and served approximately eight months before obtaining an appeal bond; the conviction was overturned in 1956 after the Supreme Court's Nelson decision. He later served a separate one-year federal sentence in 1961 and 1962 for contempt of Congress, for refusing to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee.
items.now:
Carl Braden was a trade unionist, journalist, and activist who was known for his work in the civil rights movement along with his wife Anne Braden.

In 1954, the Bradens assisted an African-American couple, Andrew and Charlotte Wade, who wanted to buy a suburban home but had been unable to do so due to housing discrimination. The Bradens purchased a house on behalf of the Wades in a white neighborhood and deeded it over to the Wade family. White segregationists immediately lashed out — burning a cross into the lawn, throwing rocks, shooting at, and eventually bombing the house. Carl Braden was charged with sedition. Although housing discrimination was illegal, the U.S. Supreme Court ruling specifically on a case in Louisville, Buchanan v. Warley, in 1917, charges were brought against Braden for hatching a communist plot to stir up a race war. A friend of the Wades was also charged with bombing the house to make it appear to have been done by others. No charges were filed regarding the other incidents. Braden rightfully denied the accusations. He was convicted on December 13, 1954, and was sentenced to 15 years in prison. His conviction was then overturned.

In 1951, when compelled to appear before the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC), Braden refused to answer questions posed to him, saying the questions violated his First Amendment rights. The House Un-American Activities Committee (also called HUAC) was a committee within the United States House of Representatives dedicated to identifying agents of Fascism or Communism, ideologies deemed "un-American". The case was heard before the Supreme Court of the United States as Braden v. United States, 365 U.S. 431 (1961). The court ruled against Braden, saying his conviction was constitutional. Braden was sentenced to a year in prison, and a drive for clemency in his case was led by Martin Luther King Jr. He was released after serving nine months of the sentence.

The Bradens were dedicated to the freedom struggle their entire lives, serving as allies willing to put everything on the line.

items.name: Kamau Sadiki
items.was: Kamau Sadiki (Freddie Hilton) is a former Black Panther and Black Liberation Army member. In 2002 he was convicted of the 1971 killing of Atlanta police officer James Greer, a cold case supporters say was revived to pressure him to inform on Assata Shakur. Gravely ill, he remains held at the Augusta State Medical Prison in Georgia.
items.now: Kamau Sadiki was a Black Panther Party member. In 1971 an Atlanta police officer was murdered while he sat in his patrol car and had his gun and badge stolen, police were unable to find any evidence leading to potential suspects but presumed the killing was committed by the local chapter of the Black Liberation Army. Police raided the groups' compound and arrested several members. While in prison one of the BLA members claimed sadiki and another man committed the shooting while attempting to make a deal with the prosecutors in order to have charges dropped. Police did not find any evidence to charge sadiki with the crime and eventually he left the world of political activism to raise his family. 30 years after the murder FBI agents contacted sadiki demanding he assist them in having Assata Shakur extradited to the united states by arranging a meeting with her where she could be arrested. After he refused he was charged with the decades old killing. In 2003 he was convicted and sentenced to life in prison.

items.name: Fran Thompson
items.was: Fran Thompson was an environmental, animal-rights, and anti-nuclear activist who shot and killed a man who had stalked and threatened her and broke into her home. Convicted of first-degree murder after being barred from presenting a self-defense argument — bias her supporters attribute to her activism — she is serving a life sentence (plus ten years) and remains imprisoned at the Women's Eastern Reception, Diagnostic and Correctional Center in Missouri.
items.now: Fran Thompson was an environmental activist in Knox County Nebraska who led a number of campaigns against District Attorney John Thomas after he convinced the Board of Supervisors to alter zoning regulations to allow a number of highly controversial projects, such as a nuclear waste dumping ground and poultry factory. During this time Thompson was being stalked by an abusive ex-boyfriend who she reported to police for threatening her life. On August 18th 1991 Thompson called police for the second time to request they provide her protection out fear her ex-boyfriend was planning to kill her. Police refused and later that night her ex-partner broke into her home and attempted to kill her. Thompson retrieved a handgun she had bought for self defense when she discovered him in the home and shot her ex-partner as he lunged at her. She then immediately called 911 to report the shooting. Thompson was initially told the case was clear self-defense and she wouldn't be charged but District Attorney John Thompson insisted on indicting her for first degree murder.  Thompson was convicted for this crime and sentenced to life in prison.

items.name: I. O. Ford
items.was: I. O. Ford was indicted in October 1954 under Kentucky sedition law in the Louisville case over aiding a Black family's move into a white neighborhood. He was jailed because he could not raise bail.
items.now:
In 2003, Sgt. Ford—serving as a counterintelligence agent with the California National Guard—reported what he described as multiple incidents of detainee abuse at a base in Samarra and requested that his allegations be formally investigated. Accounts of what happened next describe Ford being placed under close supervision and rapidly removed from Iraq via medical evacuation, with superiors framing the situation as a mental-health issue rather than initiating the investigation he requested.

The episode became part of a broader public debate about detainee treatment and whistleblower retaliation during the Iraq War. Reporting on the case also described Ford undergoing repeated evaluations that did not substantiate claims that he was psychologically unfit, while Ford asserted that the evacuation functioned to silence his allegations.

items.name: Shukri Abu-Baker
items.was: Shukri Abu-Baker was the chief executive of the Holy Land Foundation. Convicted in 2008 in the Holy Land Foundation prosecution — the largest terrorism-financing case the U.S. had then brought, built on charitable giving to Palestinians — he was sentenced to 65 years and remains imprisoned.
items.now: Hukri Abu-Baker was the president of the Holy Land Foundation, the largest Islamic charity in the United States. He spent millions building schools and hospitals in Gaza and Palestine. The Israeli government lobbied for years to have it shut down, and after 9/11, President Bush signed an executive order declaring the group a domestic terrorist organization. The government arrested its employees and argued that by building infrastructure in Palestine with charity money, it negated the need for the elected government of Palestine, which was Hamas, to build their own infrastructure. Thus, they could use the money they would have spent on hospitals instead on terrorism. After a number of mistrials and acquittals, the US government was able to convict 5 members of the board who were given sentences in 2009 that ranged from 15 to 65 years in jail. In 2009, he was sentenced to 65 years in prison.

items.name: Jacob Stachel
items.was: CPUSA Labor Secretary; head of Trade Union Unity League. Foley Square Eleven defendant; 5 years at FCI Danbury (July 1951 - March 1955).
items.now:
ONE OF ELEVEN COMMUNISTS SENTENCED UNDER DENNIS V. UNITED STATES:
Jack Stachel, a leader of the communist Workers' Party, along with ten other party leaders were found guilty for advocating the violent overthrow of the United States. None of the defendants ever directly advocated to overthrow the government, but the prosecutor claimed that by supporting an ideology that advocated for violence, they also did by extension. The defendants claimed that their First Amendment freedom of speech rights were violated and they served no "clear and present danger to the nation".

They were found guilty and each sentenced to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine. The case went all the way to the Supreme Court who affirmed the lower court's verdict.

items.name: Eric McDavid
items.was: Eric McDavid is a green anarchist who became one of the most-cited "Green Scare" entrapment cases. Convicted of conspiring to sabotage targets including the Nimbus Dam, he was sentenced to nearly 20 years — a plot prosecutors built around a young paid FBI informant, "Anna." In 2015, after the government conceded it had withheld exculpatory evidence, his conviction was vacated and he was freed after roughly nine years inside.
items.now:
Eric McDavid is a green anarchist who organized as part of an environmentalist group consisting of  Zach Jenson, Lauren Weiner, and "Anna" (Zoe Elizabeth Voss, a paid FBI informant). The group, at Voss's prompting, was planning an act of arson at Nimbus Dam. McDavid, Jenson, and Weiner were all arrested on January 13, 2006 and charged with conspiracy to destroy property by means of fire or explosives. Voss was paid over $65,000 to entrap the McDavid and specifically seduced McDavid into a romantic relationship. Jenson and Weiner also agreed to testify against McDavid in exchange for a lesser charge. McDavid was forced into almost two years in solitary confinement until after his trial. As a vegan prisoner, he engaged in numerous hunger strikes to demand equitable food.

On January 8, 2015, after he spent nine years in prison, McDavid's conviction was overturned after the prosecution conceded that the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) had withheld thousands of pages of evidence that would've exonerated McDavid.

items.name: Ed Poindexter
items.was: Edward Poindexter, with David Rice (Mondo we Langa), made up the "Omaha Two," convicted of the 1970 bombing murder of Omaha police officer Larry Minard in a COINTELPRO-tainted case that supporters long called a frame-up. He spent 52 years in prison and died in custody on December 7, 2023.
items.now: Edward Poindexter was a Vietnam war veteran and a member of the Black Panther Party who was arrested for the killing of a police officer after a 911 call was made leading police to an abandoned house that contained a suitcase outside which exploded after an officer tripped over it. The entire case against Poindexter was based on the testimony of a 16-year-old who claimed to have witnessed Poindexter and another Black Panther member build the bomb in exchange for immunity. Both men had multiple alibies during the times the witness claimed to have seen them constructing the bomb and forensic evidence presented to the jury by police of being parts of the bomb found at the men's homes was later proven to have no connection to the bomb. In 1972 Poindexter was found guilty despite a lack of physical evidence and sentenced to life in prison for the crime.

items.name: Ghassan Elashi
items.was: Ghassan Elashi was a founder and chairman of the Holy Land Foundation for Relief and Development, once the largest Muslim charity in the United States. In a case civil-liberties groups consider a landmark overreach, he was convicted in 2008 of funneling charitable donations to Palestinian committees the government linked to Hamas, and sentenced to 65 years. He remains imprisoned.
items.now: Ghassan Eashi was a Palestinian born American businessman who founded the holy land foundation which was the largest Islamic charity in the united states and spent millions building schools and hospitals in Gaza and Palestine. The Israeli government lobbied for years to have it shut down and after 9/11 president bush signed an executive order declaring the group a domestic terrorist organization. The government arrested its employees and argued that by building infrastructure in Palestine with charity money that it negated the need for the elected government of Palestinian which was Hamas to build their own infrastructure and so could use the money they would have spent on hospitals instead on terrorism. After a number of mistrials and acquittals the us government was able to convict 5 members of the board who were given sentences in 2009 that ranged from 15 to 65 years in jail. In 2009, he was sentenced to 65 years in prison.

items.name: Brandon Baxter
items.was: Brandon Baxter was one of the "Cleveland 4," Occupy activists drawn by a paid FBI informant into a manufactured 2012 plot to bomb a bridge near Cleveland with explosives the government itself supplied. Sentenced to nine years and nine months plus lifetime supervised release, he has since been released.
items.now: Brandon Baxter was an activist associated with the Occupy Cleveland movement who was arrested on April 30, 2012 following a federal investigation into an alleged plot involving explosives at the Brecksville-Northfield High Level Bridge near Cleveland, Ohio. Federal prosecutors charged Baxter with conspiracy to use a weapon of mass destruction, attempted use of a weapon of mass destruction, and malicious attempt to destroy property used in interstate commerce. Authorities framed the case as part of post-Occupy counter-terrorism efforts. Supporters and civil liberties advocates argued that the case involved FBI entrapment, asserting that an undercover informant played a central role in encouraging and directing the actions leading to Baxter’s arrest. Baxter later pleaded guilty in federal court and received a lengthy prison sentence under federal law.

items.name: Connor Stevens
items.was: Connor Stevens was one of the "Cleveland 4," entrapped by an FBI informant in a 2012 bridge-bombing sting. He was sentenced to eight years and one month plus lifetime supervised release, and was released in July 2019.
items.now: Connor Stevens was an activist involved in the Occupy Cleveland movement who was arrested on April 30, 2012 as part of a federal case centered on an alleged plan to damage the Brecksville-Northfield High Level Bridge in Ohio using explosives. Stevens was charged by the U.S. Department of Justice with conspiracy to use a weapon of mass destruction, attempted use of a weapon of mass destruction, and malicious attempt to destroy property used in interstate commerce. Federal authorities described the arrests as a terrorism prevention operation, while supporters maintained that the case relied heavily on the actions of an undercover FBI informant, raising serious concerns about entrapment. Stevens ultimately pleaded guilty and was sentenced to federal prison.

items.name: Joshua Stafford
items.was: Joshua Stafford was one of the "Cleveland 4." Unlike his co-defendants he went to trial, after lengthy questions about his mental competency, and was convicted in 2015 and sentenced to ten years plus lifetime supervised release. He has since been released.
items.now: Joshua Stafford was an activist connected to the Occupy Cleveland movement who was arrested on April 30, 2012 in connection with a federal investigation into an alleged plot involving explosives at the Brecksville-Northfield High Level Bridge near Cleveland, Ohio. Prosecutors charged Stafford with conspiracy to use a weapon of mass destruction, attempted use of a weapon of mass destruction, and malicious attempt to destroy property used in interstate commerce. While federal officials portrayed the case as a counter-terrorism success, defense attorneys and supporters argued that the plot was largely manufactured by an undercover FBI informant who steered the defendants’ actions. Stafford later pleaded guilty and received a substantial federal prison sentence.

items.name: Larry Hoover
items.was:
Larry Hoover is the founder of the Gangster Disciples. He has been imprisoned since 1973 on an Illinois murder conviction (150–200 years) and also received a federal life sentence in 1997 for running a continuing criminal enterprise. President Trump commuted the federal sentence in May 2025, but Hoover remains imprisoned on the Illinois term.

His federal sentence was commuted in May 2025 and the Bureau of Prisons records his federal release on May 29, 2025 — but he remains in Illinois state custody, serving the 200-year state murder sentence, so he is still incarcerated.
items.now: Larry Hoover is a former gang member and street level black liberation organizer currently serving concurrent sentences resulting from a prison uprising in 1978. In 1974, after the death of David Barksdale, Hoover was appointed the new leader of the BGDN. Two years later, Jerome Freeman left the BGDN, making the Black Disciples and the Black Gangster Disciples separate gang organizations. On July 22, 1978, an inmate riot at the Pontiac Correctional Center in Illinois resulted in the death of three corrections officers. This uprising was rumored to have been ordered by Hoover. 21 inmates were indicted; ten were acquitted after an 11-week trial. Charges against Hoover and seven others were eventually dropped. Hoover and the leaders of other gang organizations in Chicago came together to form the Folk Nation alliance, a pact meant to settle disputes and instill a more peaceful environment behind prison walls and on the streets. Hoover then changed the organization to GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT to move the organization onto a positive path.

items.name: Joseph Bowen
items.was: Joseph "Joe-Joe" Bowen is a Pennsylvania prisoner and longtime jailhouse organizer. Already imprisoned, he was convicted of the 1973 killings of Holmesburg Prison warden Patrick Curran and deputy warden Robert Fromhold, and has spent the decades since as a prison-movement figure.
items.now:
Joe-Joe Bowen was a BLA activist who was in prison for killing a Philadelphia police officer in a confrontation. When Joe-Joe met with his warden advocating for the better treatment of Muslim prisoners in his prison, the warden threatened his life. In retaliation, Bowen murdered the warden and deputy warden and wounded the guard commander. For this he got two life sentences.

Joe-Joe also is heavily involved with radicalizing the prison population (in his own words, "teach[ing] the brothers how to turn their rage into energy and understand their situations,”) wherever he is being held. Because of this, he has had numerous stints in solitary confinement and others measures to seperate him from the rest of the prison population.

items.name: Abdulrahman Odeh
items.was: Abdulrahman Odeh was the New Jersey representative of the Holy Land Foundation, convicted in the 2008 material-support case and sentenced to 15 years. He was released in 2020.
items.now:
Abdulrahman Odeh was a leader of the Holy Land Foundation for Relief and Development, a United States–based Muslim charity that presented itself as a major humanitarian fundraising channel for Palestinian relief. Federal authorities ultimately prosecuted Odeh and other leaders on the theory that the charity’s overseas giving and affiliated networks functioned as “material support” for Hamas.

After a federal jury conviction in 2008, Odeh was sentenced in Dallas in 2009 by Jorge A. Solis to 15 years in federal prison as part of the same case against the charity’s leadership.

items.name: Basheer Hameed
items.was: Member of the Black Liberation Army. Convicted with Abdul Majid of the April 1981 killing of NYPD officer John Scarangella in Queens, New York. Sentenced to 25 years to life and held in New York State prisons until his death in custody.
items.now:
Bashir Hameed was a Black liberation activist who worked within the Black Panther Party and later became associated with the Black Liberation Army, part of a generation that combined political organizing with a confrontationist stance toward policing and state power in the United States. His public profile grew from both movement involvement and the criminal proceedings that followed a 1981 armed confrontation with police.

He was arrested and ultimately convicted in connection with that incident, receiving a lengthy-to-life sentence. He remained incarcerated until his death in custody in 2008.

items.name: Margaret Channon
items.was:
Margaret Channon was prosecuted federally for setting fire to five Seattle Police Department vehicles during the May 30, 2020 George Floyd Uprising protests in downtown Seattle. She pleaded guilty to multiple counts of arson and was sentenced in 2022 to approximately seven years in federal prison. She is held at FCI Tallahassee.

The Bureau of Prisons records her release from federal custody on June 5, 2026.
items.now:
Margaret Aislinn Channon plead guilty to federal charges for reportedly lighting five Seattle Police Department cars on fire in the middle of a protest in Seattle during the George Floyd Uprising of 2020. She faced a prolonged case, serious state repression, and unfounded accusations from prosecutors and police throughout the course of her proceedings.

In March 2022 she was sentenced to 5 years incarceration. After 60 months' imprisonment, she will face 36 months of supervised release with special conditions. Her expected release date is June 5, 2026.

Her info and a call for support were shared in 2020 and that call for support was reiterated in summer 2022 when her sentence began.

items.name: Jeremy Hammond
items.was: Jeremy Alexander Hammond is an anarchist hacker from Chicago. As part of the Anonymous offshoot AntiSec he breached the private intelligence firm Stratfor in December 2011, and the leaked emails were published by WikiLeaks. Arrested in March 2012, he was sentenced in 2013 to the maximum ten years. He was released to a halfway house in November 2020.
items.now: Jeremy Hammond, also known by his online moniker sup_g, is an American anarchist activist and former computer hacker from Chicago. He founded the computer security training website HackThisSite in 2003. In 2012, he gained access to the servers of the private intelligence firm Strategic Forecasting (Stratfor). From viewing the internal company logs, he discovered Stratfor had spied on political activists at the behest of corporations and the U.S. government. He subsequently leaked this information to Wikileaks. In November 2013, he was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison for the data breach and release of information.

items.name: Janet Holloway Africa
items.was: Janet Holloway Africa is a member of MOVE, the Philadelphia-based Black liberation and back-to-nature group founded by John Africa, and one of the "MOVE 9." Following the August 8, 1978 armed police confrontation at MOVE's Powelton Village house — in which Officer James Ramp was killed — the nine surviving adult members were convicted of third-degree murder in 1980 and each sentenced to 30 to 100 years. After about four decades inside, consistently maintaining innocence, the MOVE 9 members were granted parole between 2018 and 2020.
items.now:
Janet Holloway Africa joined MOVE in the 1970s and became part of the group’s public-facing activism in Philadelphia, where MOVE’s “back-to-nature” communal politics—combined with outspoken resistance to police and other government authority—repeatedly drew intense conflict with officials. In later decades, she was also publicly identified with the broader campaign (by MOVE and supporters) to challenge the convictions and seek parole for imprisoned MOVE members.
Her arrest stems from the Aug. 8, 1978 confrontation at MOVE’s Powelton Village compound, which ended with the death of Officer Ramp; Holloway Africa and eight other MOVE members were convicted of third-degree murder and sentenced to decades in prison. After more than 40 years incarcerated, she was granted parole and released on May 25, 2019.

items.name: Janine Phillips Africa
items.was: Janine Phillips Africa is a member of MOVE, the Philadelphia-based Black liberation and back-to-nature group founded by John Africa, and one of the "MOVE 9." Following the August 8, 1978 armed police confrontation at MOVE's Powelton Village house — in which Officer James Ramp was killed — the nine surviving adult members were convicted of third-degree murder in 1980 and each sentenced to 30 to 100 years. After about four decades inside, consistently maintaining innocence, the MOVE 9 members were granted parole between 2018 and 2020.
items.now:
Janine Phillips Africa is similarly known as a MOVE member from the group’s high-conflict Philadelphia period in the 1970s and as one of the MOVE 9. Reporting on MOVE consistently situates her activism within the organization’s communal “back-to-nature” ideology and its direct, often confrontational stance toward city institutions—conflict that helped turn the imprisonment of the MOVE 9 into a long-running political cause for supporters.
Phillips Africa was arrested during the Aug. 8, 1978 siege/eviction confrontation at MOVE’s home and, with the other MOVE 9, was convicted of third-degree murder in Officer Ramp’s death and sentenced to decades in prison. She was granted parole and released on May 25, 2019 (the same day as Janet Holloway Africa), after spending more than 40 years incarcerated.

items.name: Mohammad El-Mezain
items.was:
Mohammad El-Mezain was a longtime Holy Land Foundation figure and its former chairman. Convicted on a conspiracy count in the 2008 material-support case, he was sentenced to 15 years. He was released around 2022 and faced immigration proceedings on release.

Mohamed El-Mezain, 55, HLF defendant; convicted at trial; 180 months federal prison.
items.now:
Mohammad El-Mezain was a senior figure in the Holy Land Foundation and became nationally known through the same long-running terrorism-finance prosecution that targeted the organization’s leadership. The case focused on the charity’s fundraising and disbursement practices—activities his supporters characterized as humanitarian advocacy—while federal prosecutors argued those activities were structured to benefit Hamas-linked institutions.

Following the 2008 convictions, El-Mezain was sentenced in 2009 to 15 years in federal prison in the same proceeding that imposed lengthy terms on multiple leaders.

items.name: Douglas L. Wright
items.was: Cleveland 4 defendant, one of the five young Occupy Cleveland activists entrapped by FBI informant Shaquille Azir in an alleged 2012 plot to bomb the Northfield Center Township bridge over the Cuyahoga River. The plot, target, financing, and dummy 'explosives' were all furnished by the informant and undercover FBI agents. Pleaded guilty in 2012 to conspiracy and attempted use of weapons of mass destruction. Sentenced in November 2012 to 11 years and 8 months in federal prison — the longest sentence of the group.
items.now: Douglas L. Wright was an activist associated with the Occupy Cleveland movement who was arrested on April 30, 2012 following a federal sting operation related to an alleged plan to damage the Brecksville-Northfield High Level Bridge in Ohio. Wright was charged with conspiracy to use a weapon of mass destruction, attempted use of a weapon of mass destruction, and malicious attempt to destroy property used in interstate commerce. Federal prosecutors characterized the case as part of national security enforcement, while critics described it as an instance of FBI entrapment, citing the prominent role of an undercover informant in proposing and facilitating the alleged plot. Wright was convicted in federal court and sentenced to a lengthy term of imprisonment.

items.name: Benjamin J. Davis Jr.
items.was:
New York City Councilman from Harlem (1943–1949) and a leading Black Communist. Convicted in the 1949 Foley Square Smith Act trial and sentenced to 5 years, which he served largely at the federal penitentiary in Terre Haute, Indiana; expelled from the City Council upon his conviction.

NYC Councilmember (Harlem) 1943-49; Harvard Law-trained attorney; CPUSA National Committee. Foley Square Eleven defendant; 5 years at FCI Terre Haute; ~3 years 4 months served; released 1955. Editor of The Worker post-release.
items.now:
ONE OF TWELVE COMMUNISTS SENTENCED UNDER DENNIS V. UNITED STATES:
Bejamin J. Davis Jr., a chairman of the communist Workers' Party, along with eleven other party leaders were found guilty for advocating the violent overthrow of the United States. None of the defendants ever directly advocated to overthrow the government, but the prosecutor claimed that by supporting an ideology that advocated for violence, they also did by extension. The defendants claimed that their First Amendment freedom of speech rights were violated and they served no "clear and present danger to the nation".
Davis spent 3 years and 4 months in federal prison plus an additional two months in jail for refusing to reveal some fellow communists.

items.name: Luke O'Donovan
items.was: Queer anarchist from Atlanta who was attacked by a group of men shouting homophobic slurs at a New Year's Eve party in East Atlanta on December 31, 2012. O'Donovan defended himself with a pocketknife, stabbing several attackers, and was charged with five counts of aggravated assault and one count of attempted murder. After more than a year of organizing by supporters, he pleaded guilty in August 2014 and was sentenced to two years in prison followed by eight years of probation, during which he was banished from Georgia outside the metro Atlanta area. His case became a rallying point for queer self-defense and anti-prison activism.
items.now:
Luke O'Donovan is a queer anarchist from Atlanta who was sentenced for stabbing the group of men (5 to 12 men) who were attacking him. In his own words: "In the early morning of January 1st, 2013, I was attacked by a group of men at a party because of my sexuality. In an attempt to defend myself from the attack I thought could end my life I stabbed 5 of them, while also being stabbed 3 times myself."

The prosecution made every effort to dismiss the case as queer-bashing, instead painting Lule as the aggressor. They went so far as to equate the term "faggot" with non-offensive terms such as "babies".

Luke was facing a sentence of up to 110 years if found guilty and so chose to accept a plea deal, which included two years in prison followed by eight years of probation in which he was banished from the state of Georgia.

items.name: Ron Porambo
items.was: Ron Porambo was a journalist who covered the 1967 Newark Riots which began when police pulled over a cab driver for flashing his high beams to a police cruiser and then brutally beat him. Over the course of the next five days police used over 13,319 rounds of live ammunition against civilians and killed 23 people. Porambo interviewed witnesses who testified that civilians killed by police had been shot indiscriminately without cause or warning. Shortly after publishing a book on the riots Porambo was the victim of a drive by shooting. A month later he shot twice in the chest by an unknown assailant while leaving a bar. Police refused to investigate the attempts on Porambos life and a police spokesperson claimed without evidence that they were publicity stunt by Porambo to promote his book. After surviving the second assassination attempt the police arrested Porambo on bribery charges for paying a police officer $50 for autopsy photos from victims of the 1967 Newark riots which he used to show that physical injuries on the bodies differed from what was claimed in police reports. Porambo was convicted on the bribery charges and sentenced to 3 months in jail.
items.now: Ron Porambo was a journalist who covered the 1967 Newark Riots. The riots began when police pulled over a cab driver for flashing his high beams to a police cruiser and then brutally beat him. Over the course of the next 5 days police used over 13,319 rounds of live ammunition against civilians and killed 23 people. Porambo's coverage differed from official accounts by interviewing witnesses who testified many of those who were killed by police had been shot indiscriminately without cause or warning. Shortly after publishing a book on the riots Porambo was the victim of a drive by shooting. A month later after surviving he was again shot at, this time being struck twice by bullets fired by an unknown assailant in the parking lot of a local bar. Police refused to investigate the attempts on Porambo's life and a police spokesperson claimed without evidence that they were publicity stunt by Porambo to promote his book. After surviving the second shooting police arrested Porambo on bribery charges for paying a police officer $50 for autopsy photos from victims of the 1967 Newark riots which he used in his reporting to point out discrepancies in police narratives for how some civilians were killed that differed from the physical injuries their bodies sustained. Porambo was convicted on the bribery charges and sentenced to 3 months in jail.

items.name: Steve Murphy
items.was: Steven James Murphy was prosecuted as an Earth Liberation Front "eco-arsonist" for a 2006 attempt to set fire to a Pasadena construction site with a homemade incendiary device. He served a five-year federal sentence and was released in February 2014.
items.now: Steve Murphy was an environmentalist activist and vegan political prisoner who wrote of his struggles obtaining equitable food in prison. He was accused of decommissioning a tractor and placing an incendiary device in a housing development construction site in the name of the Earth Liberation Front in Pasadena, CA. He was sentenced to 5 years on April 5, 2010 after pleading guilty and was released in February 2014.

items.name: Christina Reid
items.was: Christina Reid, known as Chris Reid, was an Irish republican prisoner held on United States federal charges relating to support for the Irish Republican Army, and imprisoned at FCI Pleasanton in California. Arrested on July 12, 1989, she was convicted on June 18, 1990 and sentenced on August 20, 1990 to 41 months. She entered custody in approximately June 1991 and was released on June 21, 1994. Her case was documented in the Prairie Fire Organizing Committee magazine Breakthrough.
items.now:
Christina Reid, an electronics engineer from California, was prosecuted in the Boston federal case involving alleged Irish republican weapons technology. Authorities portrayed her as part of the network supporting an effort to develop or procure equipment intended for use against British military helicopters in Northern Ireland.

Reid was convicted in the 1990 Boston trial and sentenced to roughly two and a half years in prison. Her case was often cited as an example of how the U.S. government pursued not only alleged procurement of weapons, but also the technical assistance and logistical support that could enable armed campaigns overseas.

items.name: Richard Williams
items.was: Richard Williams was a Massachusetts-born radical and Vietnam veteran who joined the United Freedom Front in the late 1970s. Arrested November 4, 1984 in Cleveland, Ohio and convicted in the 1986 Brooklyn federal trial of conspiracy, bombings, and bank robberies, receiving 45 years. In 1987 he was tried with Tom Manning for the December 21, 1981 murder of NJ State Trooper Philip Lamonaco; the first jury hung but he was retried and convicted in 1988, receiving life plus 30 years. He died of liver failure in federal custody at FMC Butner, North Carolina on December 5, 2005.
items.now:
Richard Williams was associated with the United Freedom Front and the broader U.S. radical underground of the late 1970s–1980s, a milieu in which some activists crossed from above-ground organizing into clandestine activity, including sabotage bombings and armed robberies. Williams was among the fugitives pursued in connection with that underground network.

He is most closely known for his role in a deadly encounter with law enforcement: New Jersey State Trooper Philip Lamonaco was killed during a 1981 traffic stop. Williams and fellow United Freedom Front member Thomas Manning were later convicted for the trooper’s murder and received life sentences. Williams was captured with other fugitives in 1984.

items.name: Miguel Balderos
items.was: Miguel Balderos is an anarchist convicted of an arson at the Santa Cruz, California city prosecutor's office, which he tied to protest against the city's ban on sleeping outdoors. He was released on January 9, 2016.
items.now: Miguel Balderos is an anarchist and current political prisoner who was sentenced to 10 years and 8 months in prison for the arson of the Santa Cruz, CA city prosecutor’s office. When arrested, he informed the police that he was homeless and protesting the city's cruel policies towards unhoused people, such as its ban on camping.

items.name: Roberto Rivera
items.was: Roberto Rivera was a New York-licensed physician, reportedly unemployed at the time, who was inspired by the Occupy Wall Street movement. Prosecutors said he contemplated using an explosion to topple the Charging Bull statue on Wall Street; Rivera reportedly said he abandoned the plan after determining that it could not be carried out safely. He was arrested on November 16-17, 2012 after police learned he had acquired a quantity of chemicals and raided his home. A 25-year sentence was imposed years later, reportedly in February 2019.
items.now: Roberto Rivera was an E.R hospital doctor who after becoming inspired by the Occupy Wall Street movement began stockpiling chemicals which he planned to use to vandalize and destroy the Wall Street Bull statue as an act of nonviolent protest. Police became aware he had purchased a large amount of chemicals and raided his home, arresting him for possessing items capable of being used to create explosives. Rivera admitted to his plan though maintains he had changed his mind about intending to go through with it. Despite this he was convicted on charges of possessing explosives and sentenced to 25 years in prison.

items.name: Albert Woodfox
items.was: Albert Woodfox was one of the "Angola 3." Convicted of the 1972 murder of a Louisiana State Penitentiary guard — a conviction overturned several times — he spent roughly 43 years in solitary confinement, the longest such stretch in U.S. history, before being freed on his 69th birthday in 2016 on a plea to lesser charges. His memoir "Solitary" was a Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award finalist. He died in 2022.
items.now:
Albert Woodfox is part of the Angola 3, three Black Panthers, put in solitary confinement for decades in Angola Prison,Louisiana after being framed for the death of a prison guard. Robert Hillary King has been released but Herman Wallace continues to be wrongly imprisoned alongside Albert.

In 2008 the warden of the prison stated that even if Woodfox was innocent of the murder he should still be kept in solitary because he practiced Black Pantherism and would try to organize other inmates.

items.name: Elmer Geronimo Pratt
items.was:
Decorated Vietnam paratrooper who became deputy minister of defense for the Los Angeles chapter of the Black Panther Party. He was framed for the 1968 tennis-court murder of Caroline Olsen in Santa Monica and spent 27 years in California prisons, including eight in solitary, before his conviction was vacated in 1997 on grounds that prosecutors hid that key witness Julius Butler was an FBI/LAPD informant. He won a $4.5 million civil-rights settlement in 2000.

Los Angeles Black Panther Party leader convicted of a 1968 Santa Monica murder; The Black Panther Vol. 15 (1976) refers to the conviction, which the Party regarded as an FBI COINTELPRO frame-up. He was imprisoned 27 years before the conviction was vacated in 1997. [Source: The Black Panther (Black Panther Party newspaper), v15 no.25,26; digitized at marxists.org — https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/pubs/black-panther/index.htm]
items.now: Geronimo Pratt was a decorated military veteran and a high-ranking member of the Black Panther Party. In 1970 an FBI memo would state that the FBI was constantly looking measures designed to neutralize Pratt. That year Pratt was charged with the murder of an elementary school teacher who was killed in a 1968 robbery based on the testimony of an FBI infiltrator who claimed that Pratt had privately confessed to the killing. Pratt was convicted in 1972 and sentenced to life in prison. In 1997 it was revealed that the FBI had been secretly recording Black Panther meetings in Oakland, including one that occurred at the time of the murder where Pratt was shown to be present 400 miles away from the murder in L.A. at the time it occurred. Pratt appealed on the basis that the prosecution had known about this evidence which proved he was innocent and intentionally withheld it. His conviction was finally vacated and he was released after serving 27 years in prison.

items.name: Reuben Crandall
items.was: Reuben Crandall was a physician and anti-slavery activist who organized within Washington D.C abolitionist circles. In 1835 he was arrested in Washington, D.C. after authorities found abolitionist publications in his possession and accused him of seditious libel and inciting enslaved and free Black people to revolt; the case was prosecuted by Francis Scott Key. Crandall spent months jailed before trial and was ultimately acquitted in 1836, but his imprisonment seriously damaged his health; he died a few years later in Kingston.
items.now: Crandall, a physician linked to abolitionist circles, became the target of one of the most prominent early U.S. free-speech prosecutions connected to anti-slavery literature. In 1835 he was arrested in Washington, D.C. after authorities found abolitionist publications in his possession and accused him of seditious libel and inciting enslaved and free Black people to revolt; the case was prosecuted by Francis Scott Key. Crandall spent months jailed before trial and was ultimately acquitted in 1836, but his imprisonment seriously damaged his health; he died a few years later in Kingston.

items.name: Elizabeth McAlister
items.was:
Elizabeth “Liz” McAlister is an American peace activist and former Catholic nun, long involved in anti-war and disarmament movements. She was a member of the Catholic Worker Movement and co-founder of the Jonah House community with her late husband, fellow peace activist Philip Berrigan. McAlister has participated in decades of civil disobedience against U.S. militarism and nuclear weapons dating back to the Vietnam War era.

On April 4, 2018, McAlister was one of the seven members of the Kings Bay Plowshares 7, a group of Catholic peace activists who entered the Kings Bay Naval Submarine Base in Georgia to symbolically protest the presence of Trident nuclear weapons. She was convicted in federal court on charges including trespass and destruction of government property for this action. In June 2020, McAlister was sentenced to time served, probation, and restitution for her role in the protest.
items.now:
Elizabeth “Liz” McAlister (born November 17, 1939) is an American peace activist and former Catholic nun, long involved in anti-war and disarmament movements. She was a member of the Catholic Worker Movement and co-founder of the Jonah House community with her late husband, fellow peace activist Philip Berrigan. McAlister has participated in decades of civil disobedience against U.S. militarism and nuclear weapons dating back to the Vietnam War era.

On April 4, 2018, McAlister was one of the seven members of the Kings Bay Plowshares 7, a group of Catholic peace activists who entered the Kings Bay Naval Submarine Base in Georgia to symbolically protest the presence of Trident nuclear weapons. She was convicted in federal court on charges including trespass and destruction of government property for this action. In June 2020, McAlister was sentenced to time served, probation, and restitution for her role in the protest.

items.name: Carmen Trotta
items.was:
Carmen Trotta is an American pacifist and prominent activist in the Catholic Worker Movement. He has been involved in anti-war protests for decades, including opposition to the Iraq War, work with War Resisters League, and co-founding the faith-based group Witness Against Torture.

Trotta was one of the Kings Bay Plowshares 7 who on April 4, 2018 entered the Kings Bay Naval Submarine Base in Georgia to symbolically protest the U.S. nuclear arsenal. He was convicted in federal court alongside his co-defendants for trespassing and destroying government property. Trotta was sentenced to 14 months in prison for his role in the action, though he served about six months before early release, consistent with the tradition among Plowshares activists of accepting prison as part of their witness against war and nuclear weapons.

items.name: Kimberly Rivera
items.was:
Kimberly Rivera is an American Iraq War resister and former U.S. Army Private First Class. After serving roughly a year in the Army and deploying to Iraq, she went AWOL (absent without leave) in February 2007, citing moral and religious objections to the Iraq War and her participation in it. She fled to Canada, becoming the first female U.S. military deserter to seek refuge there. Amnesty International designated her a prisoner of conscience in recognition of her conscientious objection to war.

In September 2012, Canadian authorities deported Rivera back to the United States, where she pleaded guilty to desertion. She received a bad-conduct discharge from the U.S. Army and was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment. Her case drew international attention from peace activists and human rights groups who opposed the prosecution of conscientious objectors.

items.name: Ben Salmon
items.was: Ben Salmon was one of the most visible U.S. conscientious objectors of World War I, arguing from Catholic pacifist convictions that participation in war was morally impossible. On June 5, 1917, he wrote directly to President Wilson refusing to register for the draft on the grounds that all war was incompatible with the teachings of Christ; he was sentenced to death, which was reduced to 25 years hard labor for desertion and "spreading propaganda," and imprisoned at Fort Leavenworth. In 1920 he launched a hunger strike over his treatment and was transferred to St. Elizabeths Hospital; public pressure for the release of wartime objectors grew, and he was pardoned and freed in November 1920. His ordeal permanently broke his health; he died of pneumonia in 1932 at age 43.
items.now: Ben Salmon became one of the most visible U.S. conscientious objectors of World War I, arguing from Catholic pacifist convictions that participation in war was morally impossible. His refusal to cooperate with the draft and induction process led to arrest and a military court-martial in 1918; he was sentenced to 25 years of hard labor (after an initial death sentence was reduced) and imprisoned at Fort Leavenworth. In 1920 he launched a hunger strike over his treatment and was transferred to St. Elizabeths Hospital; public pressure for the release of wartime objectors grew, and he was pardoned and freed in November 1920. His ordeal—years of confinement and coercive punishment despite the war’s end—became a reference point in later conscientious-objection and antiwar movements.

items.name: Raphael Joseph
items.was: Note to editors: This seems not to fit your definition of a political prisoner. He murdered eight white people in the Virgin Islands due to white resentment (which is political, but the murders could hardly be described as political). He did not receive an abnormally long sentence (eight life sentences for murdering eight people), and if he did, he was not a political activist or anything; there was not anything inherently political about him or his case.

items.name: Abdul Majid
items.was: Abdul Majid is a native of Queens New York and has been imprisoned for two decades. In the 1960s, he worked in the Grass Roots Advisory Council, an anti-poverty program. In the late 60s Abdul joined the Black Panther Party and the Republic of New Afrika. Abdul was involved in many of the community-based programs of the BPP including the free health clinic, free breakfast for children program, and efforts to decentralize the public schools and the police department. After the BPP was destroyed by the FBI’s COINTELPRO program, Abdul worked as a paralegal at Bronx Legal Services.

what: For every prisoner whose Airtable description is longer than the one on the site, the site description is replaced with the Airtable text. 51 records, 29,931 characters gained.
reversibility: Every replaced description is stored verbatim in this payload under was. That is the entire rollback: the current site text is not recoverable from anywhere else once this runs, because it is not the Airtable text and the Airtable is not versioned. If any of these reads worse afterwards, the old wording is here.
the_tradeoff: Worth stating plainly, because it is a real change of register. The site descriptions are short, dated, third-person summaries written in the archives own voice. The Airtable descriptions are the campaign copy they were condensed from: longer, richer in circumstance, and in places openly advocating -- Zolo still adamantly maintains innocence, He is a very peaceful and deeply spiritual person. That is what these pages will now say. The curator asked for the longer text and the longer text is what carries the detail, but nobody should be surprised later that the tone moved.
paragraphs_note: The Airtable text is stored raw, with its newlines intact. 320 of the 572 Airtable descriptions contain real line breaks, and the prisoner page splits the description on newline and renders each part as its own paragraph -- so these will lay out as multi-paragraph biographies rather than as one block. Zolo Azania becomes seventeen paragraphs, Maliki Shakur Latine fifteen. Collapsing that whitespace would have produced a wall of text.
no_data_moves: Only the description column is touched. No dates, no case rows, no photos, no names. Where the Airtable prose contains dates the structured fields already hold -- Latines birth date, for one -- the fields stay authoritative and unchanged.
kambui_note: One record is matched through the AKA field: the Airtable calls him William J. Turk, the archive calls him Sekou Kambui. Checked before including it -- the Airtable prose itself calls him Sekou Kambui throughout, so only the Airtable row label uses the birth name. The text will read correctly on his page.
